summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\) to show both sums vanish modulo \(p\) for \(p\le n<2p\); at \(n=p-1\), \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives the first boundary value \(1\), while divisibility of \(\binom{2k}{k}\) eliminates every term but \(k=(p-1)/2\) in the second, giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Thus each Hankel matrix is zero beyond its anti-diagonal, so only the reversing permutation survives in the determinant expansion; its sign is \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), which directly gives the first result and cancels the anti-diagonal product in the second.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                  \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},
\]
so that \(p=2m+1\). All congruences in the proof are modulo \(p\), or equivalently identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We will prove four sequence identities:
\[
 a(n)\equiv0,\qquad c(n)\equiv0\quad (p\le n<2p),                 \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 a(p-1)\equiv1,\qquad c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.                       \tag{2}
\]
After that, a general determinant argument will finish the proof.

We repeatedly use the following form of Lucas's theorem. If
\(N=N_0+pN_1\) and \(K=K_0+pK_1\), where \(0\le N_0,K_0<p\), then
\[
 \binom NK\equiv \binom{N_0}{K_0}\binom{N_1}{K_1}\pmod p.       \tag{3}
\]
Only numbers smaller than \(3p\) occur below, so this two-digit form is enough. It follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\((1+X)^N=(1+X)^{N_0}((1+X)^p)^{N_1}\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), using
\((1+X)^p=1+X^p\).

In particular, if \(p\le n<2p\), then for every \(0\le k\le n\),
\[
 \binom nk\equiv\binom{n\bmod p}{k\bmod p}.                      \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the leading base-\(p\) digit of \(n\) is \(1\), while that of \(k\) is either \(0\) or \(1\); hence the second factor in (3) is either \(\binom10\) or \(\binom11\), both equal to \(1\).

We also need two consequences concerning central binomial coefficients. Write
\[
 B(t)=\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
If \(0\le t<p\) and \(2t\ge p\), then
\[
 B(t)\equiv0.                                                     \tag{5}
\]
To see this, write \(2t=p+s\), where \(0\le s<p\). Since \(t<p\), Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 B(t)\equiv \binom{s}{t}\binom10.
\]
Here \(s=2t-p<t\), so \(\binom{s}{t}=0\).

For \(0\le y<p\), Lucas's theorem also gives
\[
 B(p+y)\equiv B(y)\left(2+\left\lfloor\frac{2y}{p}\right\rfloor\right). \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the lower number \(p+y\) has base-\(p\) digits \((y,1)\). The lower digit of \(2(p+y)\) is \(2y\bmod p\), and its next digit is
\(2+\lfloor2y/p\rfloor\). Applying Lucas once gives
\[
B(p+y)\equiv
 \binom{2y\bmod p}{y}\binom{2+\lfloor2y/p\rfloor}{1}.
\]
A second application of Lucas to \(B(y)\), noting that the leading digit of \(y\) is zero, gives
\[
B(y)\equiv\binom{2y\bmod p}{y},
\]
which proves (6).

A useful symmetry now follows. If \(0\le x,y<p\) and \(x+y<p\), then
\[
 B(x)B(p+y)\equiv B(p+x)B(y).                                    \tag{7}
\]
By (6), this is equivalent to
\[
B(x)B(y)\left(2+\left\lfloor\frac{2y}{p}\right\rfloor\right)
=
B(x)B(y)\left(2+\left\lfloor\frac{2x}{p}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
If the two floor values agree, this is immediate. They cannot both be \(1\), because that would imply \(x+y\ge p\). If exactly one is \(1\), say \(\lfloor2y/p\rfloor=1\), then \(2y\ge p\), and (5) says \(B(y)=0\); hence both sides vanish. The other case is symmetric. Thus (7) holds in every case.

We next prove the vanishing assertions (1). Let \(p\le n<2p\), and write
\[
 n=p+r,
 \qquad 0\le r<p.
\]
For \(0\le k<p\), formula (4) says
\[
\binom nk\equiv\binom rk.
\]
Consequently this is zero when \(r<k<p\). For \(0\le x\le r\), formula (4) also gives
\[
 \binom n{x}\equiv\binom rx,
 \qquad
 \binom n{p+x}\equiv\binom rx.                                  \tag{8}
\]
Thus every nonzero term in the sum defining \(a(n)\) belongs to a pair indexed by \(x\) and \(p+x\), with \(0\le x\le r\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
 (-1)^{p+x}=-(-1)^x.
\]
Using (8), the two terms in each pair are negatives of one another:
\[
(-1)^x\binom nx^4+(-1)^{p+x}\binom n{p+x}^4
\equiv
(-1)^x\binom rx^4-(-1)^x\binom rx^4=0.
\]
This proves \(a(n)\equiv0\).

The same partition of the summation indices works for \(c(n)\). Again, all terms with \(r<k<p\) vanish because their factor \(\binom nk^2\) is zero. Fix \(0\le x\le r\) and put \(y=r-x\). The term indexed by \(x\) is, by (8),
\[
 T_x\equiv (-1)^x\binom rx^2 B(x)B(p+y),                          \tag{9}
\]
because \(n-x=p+r-x=p+y\). The term indexed by \(p+x\) is
\[
 T_{p+x}\equiv-(-1)^x\binom rx^2 B(p+x)B(y),                     \tag{10}
\]
because \(n-(p+x)=r-x=y\). Here \(x+y=r<p\), so (7) says that the products of central binomial coefficients in (9) and (10) are equal. Therefore \(T_x+T_{p+x}=0\). Summing these cancellations for \(0\le x\le r\) proves \(c(n)\equiv0\), completing (1).

We now evaluate the two boundary values in (2). First recall the familiar congruence
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\qquad(0\le k<p).                     \tag{11}
\]
For completeness, it follows directly from
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}= rac{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}{k!}
\equiv\frac{(-1)(-2)\cdots(-k)}{k!}=(-1)^k,
\]
since \(k!\) is invertible modulo \(p\).

Using (11),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
&\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
As \(p\) is odd, the alternating sum of \(p\) terms is \(1\). Hence
\[
 a(p-1)\equiv1.                                                   \tag{12}
\]

For \(c(p-1)\), its \(k\)-th summand is
\[
(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^2 B(k)B(p-1-k).                             \tag{13}
\]
We show that only the middle index \(k=m\) contributes. If \(k<m\), then
\(t=p-1-k\) satisfies \(t<p\) and \(2t\ge p\), so (5) gives
\(B(p-1-k)=0\). If \(k>m\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so (5) gives \(B(k)=0\). Thus all terms except \(k=m\) vanish.

At \(k=m\), one has \(p-1-m=m\) and \(2m=p-1\), so both central binomial factors equal \(\binom{p-1}{m}\). Therefore (13) becomes
\[
 (-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2
 \binom{p-1}{m}\binom{p-1}{m}
 =(-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^4.
\]
By (11), \(\binom{p-1}{m}\equiv(-1)^m\), whose fourth power is \(1\). Hence
\[
 c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.                                              \tag{14}
\]
Together, (12) and (14) prove (2).

It remains to explain the determinant reduction. We use the following elementary lemma.

**Anti-diagonal determinant lemma.** Let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) be a matrix over any commutative ring, and suppose
\[
 M_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i+j\ge p.                           \tag{15}
\]
Then
\[
 \det M=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho)\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}M_{\rho(j),j},   \tag{16}
\]
where \(\rho(j)=p-1-j\) is the reversal permutation.

Indeed, expand the determinant as a sum over permutations \(\sigma\):
\[
 \det M=\sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
              \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}M_{\sigma(j),j}.
\]
Suppose a term is potentially nonzero. By (15), it is then necessary that
\[
 \sigma(j)+j\le p-1\qquad\text{for every }j.                     \tag{17}
\]
On the other hand, because \(\sigma\) permutes \(0,1,\dots,p-1\),
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}(\sigma(j)+j)
=2\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}j
=p(p-1).
\]
There are \(p\) summands in this last sum, and each is at most \(p-1\) by (17). Since their sum is exactly \(p(p-1)\), every one must equal \(p-1\). Thus \(\sigma(j)=p-1-j\) for every \(j\), so \(\sigma=\rho\). Every other permutation has at least one factor with row plus column at least \(p\), and its term is zero. This proves (16).

The sign of reversal is
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}(\rho)=(-1)^m.                                \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, because \(p=2m+1\), reversal is the product of the \(m\) disjoint transpositions
\[
 (0,p-1)(1,p-2)\cdots(m-1,m+1),
\]
and it fixes \(m\). Each transposition has sign \(-1\), proving (18).

Now let
\[
 A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p},\qquad
 C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reduce their entries modulo \(p\). Since \(0\le i,j<p\), one always has
\(i+j<2p\). If \(i+j\ge p\), (1) therefore gives
\[
 a(i+j)\equiv c(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus both reduced matrices satisfy the hypothesis of the anti-diagonal determinant lemma. Reduction modulo \(p\) commutes with the additions and multiplications in the determinant expansion, so it is enough to compute their determinants in \(\mathbb F_p\).

Every entry on the anti-diagonal of \(A\) has index
\[
 \rho(j)+j=(p-1-j)+j=p-1.
\]
By (12), every such entry is \(1\). Applying (16) and (18), we obtain
\[
 \det A\equiv(-1)^m\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}1=(-1)^m
 =(-1)^{(p-1)/2}.
\]
This is the first claimed congruence.

Likewise, every anti-diagonal entry of \(C\) is \(c(p-1)\), which equals \((-1)^m\) modulo \(p\) by (14). Therefore
\[
\det C
\equiv(-1)^m\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}(-1)^m
=(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^m\). Consequently
\[
 \det C\equiv(-1)^m(-1)^m=(-1)^{2m}=1.
\]
This proves the second claimed congruence and completes the proof.
